newsitem.title: FRANCE: France asked for help to share out Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: France asked for help to share out Nazi gold.

text.p: An official of the Simon Weisenthal Centre was in Paris on Thursday to seek French President Jacques Chirac's backing for a plant to share out among war victims the last Nazi gold still being held by the World War Two allies.

"We need a political decision by President Chirac and I hope we will have it when we meet (senior Chirac aide) Jean-David Levitte later today," Rabbi Abraham Cooper, associate dean of the U.S.-based Nazi-hunting group, said.
At stake are 5.5 tonnes of gold jointly held by The United States, Britain and France and stored in London and New York.
It is all that remains of 377 tonnes looted by the Nazis, recovered at the end of the war and since re-distributed by a Tripartite Gold Commission (TGC).
TGC policy was to distribute gold among states, excluding individual victims in what Cooper says was "a major rip-off".

"Some gold came from national banks looted by the Nazis. But much was from victims - privately held gold, jewellry, wedding bands and, yes, gold teeth the Nazis wrenched from the mouths of their victims after gassing them to death," he told Reuters.

The Weisenthal Centre has asked Washington, London and Paris to change TGC policy and share out the last 5.5 tonnes, primarily among ageing concentration camp survivors whatever their nationality or religion.
"This is not charity. This is a matter of reassigning property that people really owned," he said.

Cooper said British Foreign Office Permanent Undersecretary of State Liam Fox told him in London last week he could count on Britain's support but the change would also have to be approved by the United States and France.

"We are somewhat surprised that we have heard nothing from President Clinton yet, and we hope Monsieur Chirac, president of a country which suffered deeply from the war will understand how important this issue is," he said.

Nazi loot is also an issue in France where Prime Minister Alain Juppe told Jewish leaders on Saturday he would set up a commission to clarify the status of property never returned to its rightful owners after the war, mostly because they were killed in gas chambers.
A recent book said French authorities took over from the retreating Germans in 1944, and still administered, possibly hundreds of flats left vacant by Jews killed in death camps.
A government body also determined that nearly 2,000 works of art, possibly seized from Jews, were still "provisionally" in care of French museums more than 50 years after the war.

Juppe's announcement also followed moves to shed light on the dark years of World War Two in other countries including neutral Switzerland and Sweden, which both have been accused of profitably dealing with the Nazis and being paid in gold seized from their victims.
